# Compliance

This file describes what the software does and where its safeguards live. It is not legal
advice, and it does not decide anything on your behalf. If you run this for anyone other than
yourself, the obligations are yours.

## Transparency: content generated by a model

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act) has applied since 2 August 2026 (Article 113;
Article 50 sits in Chapter IV and is in none of the deferred groups).

**There is no open question about whether the free and open-source exemption covers this.**
Article 2(12) exempts AI systems released under free and open-source licences *"unless they
are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that
falls under Article 5 or 50"*. Article 50 is carved out of the exemption by name.

Two duties in Article 50 reach this system, and they fall on different people:

- **Article 50(2) — on the provider.** Outputs of an AI system generating synthetic text
  must be *"marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or
  manipulated"*.
- **Article 50(4), second subparagraph — on the deployer.** Whoever deploys an AI system
  that generates text *"published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of
  public interest"* must disclose that the text was artificially generated. That is this
  product's exact purpose. The provision exempts content that *"has undergone a process of
  human review or editorial control"* with a person holding editorial responsibility —
  **this system does not qualify for that exemption and says so in the data**:
  `human_verified` is `false` and no path sets it to anything else.

Article 50(5) adds that the information must reach the person *"in a clear and
distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure"* and
*"conform to the applicable accessibility requirements"*.

Where these are satisfied:

- The API cannot serve an analysis without also serving its provenance. `Provenance` carries
  `ai_generated: true`, `human_verified: false`, the model name, the prompt version and the
  timestamp (`src/api/schemas.py`). It is a required field of the article detail response —
  a client that renders an analysis has already received it.
- The interface renders it beside every analysis: *"Analysis generated by a model. Nobody has
  checked it."* plus model, prompt version and date, taken from the data rather than written
  into the page (`web/components/provenance-note.tsx`).
- Accuracy is disclosed in the same view as the findings, not in a file nobody opens
  (`reliability` in `web/messages/`). See [MODEL_CARD.md](MODEL_CARD.md).

**Known gap: the accessibility half of Article 50(5) has not been tested.** The note renders
beside every analysis, which satisfies "first exposure"; whether it meets the accessibility
requirements referenced there has not been assessed, and this file will not claim it does.

**What your deployment may add.** Scale, purpose and context can bring further obligations —
including ones that do not apply to the software as distributed. Assess your own deployment.

## Text and data mining reservations

Article 4 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 lets a rightsholder reserve their content against text
and data mining. **A deployment in Poland is bound by the transposition, not by the
directive**: the Act of 26 July 2024 (Dz.U. 2024 poz. 1254, in force 20 September 2024)
inserted `art. 26³` into the Polish copyright act. Three of its terms matter here:

- **`art. 26³ ust. 1`** — reproduction of disseminated works for the purpose of text and data
  mining is permitted *"chyba że uprawniony zastrzegł inaczej"* (unless the rightsholder has
  reserved otherwise).
- **`art. 26³ ust. 2`** — for works made publicly available online, the reservation must be
  made *"w formacie przeznaczonym do odczytu maszynowego"* together with metadata.
- **`art. 26³ ust. 3`** — works reproduced under this exception *may be stored only for the
  purpose of text and data mining, and only for as long as that purpose requires*.

`art. 6 ust. 1 pkt 22` defines the mining itself as automated analysis *"w celu wygenerowania
określonych informacji, obejmujących w szczególności wzorce, tendencje i korelacje"*.

The `sources` table carries `tdm_reserved` as **data**, and the seeded row for `Gazeta.pl`
sets it: that outlet's `robots.txt` reserves mining in prose that reproduces the statutory
definition almost word for word — it is aimed at this activity, not at crawling in general.
Its crawl directives permit the feed and the feed parses correctly; that is not the question.
Whether prose inside `robots.txt` satisfies the machine-readable form `ust. 2` requires is a
live question, and **this project does not need to answer it, because the source ships off.**

**`ust. 3` constrains retention, and no code here enforces it.** An operator relying on this
exception is storing headlines and leads under a statutory purpose limit. Nothing in this
repository expires them; see *Personal data* below.

**Every source ships disabled.** Enabling one is an explicit act by an operator who has
looked at that publisher's terms. This project takes no position on which sources you may
collect from, and shipping active defaults would have taken one.

## Personal data

If you enable accounts, you are the controller for the data your users leave: an email
address, a password hash, session records, saved articles and category subscriptions.

The code provides deletion that cascades across all four tables, Argon2id hashing, and
session tokens stored only as SHA-256 digests. It does **not** provide a retention schedule
or email verification. Those are deployment decisions and neither is made for you.

**Articles 15 and 20 are answered by the person, not by you.** `GET /me/export` returns
everything the account holds as JSON — address, creation time, session timestamps, saved
articles, followed categories — and the account page links to it. Credentials are excluded on
purpose: the password hash is offline-attackable and a session digest is a live token, and
neither answers a question the timestamps do not.

**What is collected from publishers is a URL, a headline and a lead — never the article
body.** There is no column for it: see `articles` in `migrations/001_init.sql`. That is a far
smaller footprint than a corpus of full texts, and it is worth stating precisely rather than
overclaiming. Headlines and leads still name people, so they still carry personal data.
Retention of that corpus is your decision and nothing here expires it — which, where you rely
on the Polish text-and-data-mining exception, is a limit you have to implement yourself
(`art. 26³ ust. 3`, above).

## What the product says, and about whom

**Every claim is about a sentence. None is about a newsroom.** The interface reports a quoted
fragment and a technique; it never aggregates by outlet, never ranks publishers, and never
states that an outlet manipulates. This is a deliberate constraint on the product, not an
accident of the current screens — aggregate views exist only as operator diagnostics of the
model, and there is no public API, because a machine-readable endpoint serving everything
makes the constraint unenforceable.

Two mechanisms keep it honest:

- **A quote that cannot be located in the source text is discarded, always.** There is no
  repair heuristic and none may be added. A tool that names outlets cannot cite sentences
  they never published — and this is also the only defence against prompt injection that does
  not depend on the model's cooperation.
- **The model is never told which outlet published the text.** With outlets of opposing
  political profiles on one list, brand recognition shifts the output: labelling the source
  raised the number of accusations by about a third and lowered their accuracy.

Fewer than half the findings hold up (see [MODEL_CARD.md](MODEL_CARD.md)). Presenting this
output as a verdict about a publication would be both wrong and, depending on where you are,
actionable. The interface presents each finding as an observation with its source link, and
states the measured accuracy in the same view.

## Model weights

No weights are distributed here. The operator pulls the model from their own Ollama
installation, under whatever licence that model carries. This project neither grants nor
restricts any right in it, and the model named in [MODEL_CARD.md](MODEL_CARD.md) is a default,
not a requirement.

The default was checked rather than assumed: `ollama show gemma4:latest --license` returns
the Apache License 2.0 and nothing else — no acceptable-use addendum and no prohibited-use
policy attached. **Check the licence of whatever model you actually run**, because a
substitute may carry use restrictions that this one does not, and swapping the model is a
supported operation (see [OPERATOR.md](OPERATOR.md)).

## Cyber Resilience Act

Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 applies from **11 December 2027**, with Article 14 (reporting)
from 11 September 2026 and Chapter IV from 11 June 2026.

Its two relevant roles are drawn narrowly. A *manufacturer* places a product on the market
in the course of a commercial activity. An *open-source software steward* is defined in
Article 3 as **a legal person**, other than a manufacturer, systematically supporting the
development of free and open-source software *"intended for commercial activities"*, and
carries the duties in Article 24 — a documented cybersecurity policy and cooperation with
market surveillance authorities.

**Publishing this repository non-commercially fits neither role.** If you monetise a
deployment, or a legal person takes over sustained stewardship of it for commercial
purposes, that changes and Article 24 is where to start reading.

## Untrusted input

Article text is treated as untrusted for the whole pipeline. It stays inside nonce-delimited
tags in the user turn, is never concatenated into the system prompt, and is never edited to
strip instruction-like phrasing — editing it would alter the material being assessed.

Cloud providers, where configured, are restricted to zero-data-retention endpoints, because
the article text being sent is exactly this untrusted third-party content.
